description_full: Vicor Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, designs, develops, manufactures, and markets modular power components and power systems for converting electrical power for use in electrically powered devices in the United States, Europe, the Asia Pacific, and internationally. The company offers a range of brick-format DC-DC converters; complementary components that provide AC line rectification, input filtering, power factor correction, and transient protection; and input and output voltage, and output power products, as well as sells electrical and mechanical accessories. It also designs, sells, and services custom power system solutions. It serves independent manufacturers of electronic devices, original equipment manufacturers, original design manufacturers, and their contract manufacturers in the aerospace and aviation, defense electronics, satellites, factory automation, instrumentation, test equipment, transportation, telecommunications and networking infrastructure, and vehicle markets. Vicor Corporation was incorporated in 1981 and is headquartered in Andover, Massachusetts.
ceo_bio: Dr. Patrizio  Vinciarelli Ph.D. | Founder, Chairman, CEO & President | Age 78 | Compensation: $541,960 (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 1K people. Revenue per employee of $415K ranks in the above the sector median among Technology peers. Each employee generates $109K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $15K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 1× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (6/10).
financial_summary: Vicor Corporation is a mid-cap technology business with a $7.3B market cap on $453M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 16% against a 11% cost of capital, a 5-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 45%.

The business throws off $119M in free cash flow — roughly 26 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.18× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 40× is fortress-like.
Shareholder yield is only 0.5%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 25% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

sect: Its 18% operating margin runs 11pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.77x).
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+16.8% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 533 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 202% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 27% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 58% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 98% and a beta of 1.36, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 3.58 vs 5y 2.01), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $188.4M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 42% in the 2020 crash, 64% in the 2022 bear market and 74% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $44.98 (margin of safety -254%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 37%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $30.06 to $71.98 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Technology peers: P/E 41.5 vs 27.4, EV/EBITDA 42.7 vs 17.1 and P/FCF 61.6 vs 26.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 2% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 1.6% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 1.2% (vs the 8% bar).
The 4 covering analysts target $390 on average, 145% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 16% earns above the cost of capital of 11.2%, but the 5pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 2.62).
It runs a 45% gross margin and converts 26% of revenue into free cash flow, or 23% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.18x.
ROE of 17% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.1x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 11pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 17.4% of revenue on R&D and 3.7% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $402.8M (5% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 62.0, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 198 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.3% over 3 years, 8.8% over 5 years and 7.5% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 14%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 16.0% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 82.5% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.0x, 4.5% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 31, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 25.1%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 67%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (100 sales, net $24.0M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.5% (0.5% in buybacks).
The share count has grown 1.3% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
Short interest is elevated at 10.2% of the float, 1.9 days to cover.
people: With about 1,092 employees, each generates about $415K of revenue, in line with the Technology median, and revenue has grown 4.2% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $109K of free cash flow per employee.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
CEO pay is $542K (1x revenue per employee).
